findings.reason: The protected Python solution finds the lowest common ancestor (LCA) of target nodes p and q in a binary tree where targets may be absent. It uses a postorder DFS helper search(node) that returns (candidate, found_count). It combines subtree counts with current node identity checks and only returns the candidate if found_count == 2. The solution runs in O(n) time and O(h) space; no candidate is required.
Postorder traversal checks target presence across both left and right subtrees. Returning candidate only when found_count == 2 ensures null is returned if either p or q is absent.
Visiting all n tree nodes once takes O(n) time. Recursion stack uses O(h) space where h is tree height. Complexity evidence is inherited and hash-bound.
Accepts root, p, and q TreeNode objects, returning the LCA TreeNode if both exist in root or None.

The approach accurately details postorder DFS returning structural candidate and target count, single-pass existence verification, root count threshold validation, and O(n) time / O(h) space bounds. Alternatives and edge cases cover separate membership scans overhead, parent pointer ancestor set extra space, repeated subtree membership search quadratic costs, self-ancestor targets, absent target null returns, distinct node identities, and single-node tree limits.

App Python and native Python solutions both execute the identical postorder DFS target-count LCA algorithm with SHA-256 digests 9edf0093d653b9d32ccd3b59d9d1165fd9c848c2da34d39cc3fbe3318c69125f and 161f9eb09d1dfdeacab3e29659e3c8022f35ebea592a946388b21740963a487a.
